segments.title: THE STARTER THAT TAKES ITS SOUR
notes: It's Never Too Late To Change
segments.angle: What if this problem existed in an entirely different industry?

sources.text: The Influence Of Others: You are the average of the five people you spend the most time with
It's Never Too Late To Change: No matter how old you are, it's never too late to make a change in your life.
The Influence Of Others: Be with people who see the world in the bigger picture so that THAT becomes your normal frame of mind.
The Choice To Change Is Ours: Either curse the world for being unfair or do all that you can to improve yourself, no matter how little.
The Influence Of Others: Live among your fellow freaks, where obsession is normal and ambition is rewarded.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Last part. Influence and change, in one jar. Go on, then.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A sourdough starter, March. It takes its sour from whoever feeds it, and those five people become its whole flavour.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Bakery now. Fine, we're in a bakery.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And a starter that was sour yesterday can be fed fresh today. It is never too late for the dough.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fresh feed doesn't rise if the jar still sits on the windowsill next to the bins.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then move the jar. Keep it among bakers who bake before dawn, and rising becomes the normal frame of mind.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine. Good one. Moving the jar is the easy half.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The hard half is choosing to feed it at all, rather than cursing the windowsill for being unfair.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Curse the windowsill, feed the starter. Right, and the bakery isn't fair either.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Live among your fellow freaks, March. Bakers obsessed with rising dough are normal there, and ambition is rewarded.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Obsessed bakers get up in the dark. Nobody mentions that part.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ambition gets rewarded, March. The bread is the reward.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Verdict. You were right that the jar matters. I was right that the feeding does the work.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then we agree on the crust, March. Allow me to sit in your chair and deliver the verdict properly.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Sit in that and you'll go flat by lunch.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: And Warden of the Graft-Yard? Pick a title that doesn't smell of yeast.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Destiny has a smell, March, and it is yeast. Sit with it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Up next, Your Routine Is Top Priority. Bring flour.

segments.title: THE ROPE THAT FRAYS IN CALM WEATHER
segments.angle: Imagine this idea has been implemented and failed spectacularly one year from now. What are the most likely reasons for its failure? How could we mitigate those risks now?

sources.text: Your Routine Is Top Priority: Obey your schedule, no matter how you feel. It doesn't matter how far along you are with something or how much left needs to be done. The moment it's time for the next activity to start, you MUST switch over.
Your Routine Is Top Priority: A schedule makes you act according to the goals of your highest self, not your passing mood.
Your Routine Is Top Priority: If you have a problem with the schedule then change the schedule itself, not self revise the schedule on a day by day basis.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Your Routine Is Top Priority. Bossy title. It wants us all obeying the timetable like a bus driver with a grudge.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A timetable is a ship's log, March. Every hour is written before the storm, and the crew keeps to it through the worst weather.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Storms don't read logs. Try it on me. One year on, the whole thing has failed spectacularly. I'd switch over mid-sentence every time and hate it by spring.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then you are the first casualty, March, and the rest of the crew sails on. A schedule makes you act according to your highest self, not your passing mood.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Highest self, passing mood. Lovely. Tell that to a Tuesday when the mood is the only thing talking. Failure one: it was built for the good days and has no plan for the bad.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the schedule is a mooring, March. A boat holds fast through a gale because the line was fixed before the wind arrived.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A mooring line doesn't snap in a gale. It snaps in calm weather, frayed at one knot nobody bothered to check. That's the failure I'd bet on.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Such a simple knot, March. Routine is simple, and simple things endure.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Simple? Nothing about that knot is simple. Another failure: when it chafes, the note says change the whole schedule, not nudge it. So nobody nudges anything, and the rope rots.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You bristle at the word simple like a cat at a bath, March. Yet you have described my mooring exactly.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You have stolen my rope, March, and I resent every frayed thread of it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Stolen? I handed it back. Keep it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then allow me to crown J the Keeper of the Mooring. A title worthy of a man who holds fast.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: He can have a title when he's got a loose rope to hold. Keeper of the Line, honestly. Pick a smaller one.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Smaller is for shopkeepers, March. Keepers are for ships.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Round one goes to the rule being untested, not wrong. Mitigation: build the bad-day version before the storm, not after.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I shall keep the knot in my pocket, March, and you may keep your bad-day version. We meet again at the mooring.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Next up, the other half of this one. Bring the rope, and don't fray it on the way.

segments.title: THE SWITCH THAT NEVER WAITS
segments.angle: What would this idea look like if I went to its extreme? Could that open up anything interesting?

sources.text: Routine Is Top Priority: Obey your schedule, no matter how you feel.
Routine Is Top Priority: The moment it's time for the next activity to start, you MUST switch over.
Routine Is Top Priority: Following your schedule is the most overpowered thing you can do because it turns your entire perfect day into a habit.
Routine Is Top Priority: If you have a problem with the schedule then change the schedule itself, not self revise the schedule on a day by day basis.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Run the extreme. Obey the schedule no matter how I feel. Fine. Feel nothing, switch on the dot.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ah, March, you propose to sail with the wind tied up in the hold. A bold course, though a pale one, and I doubt the ship would enjoy it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Bell rings. I drop the word I was holding. Half a word left in the air.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A bus pulled away from the corner this morning at the exact minute its board promised, and I saw in it the quiet proof that the world keeps its appointments. Some things are meant to be punctual, March, and a half-finished word is simply a word that was never going to be finished.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A bus is a bus. Extreme version: I finish nothing, ever. That's the whole rule.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You make a fine poor example, March, and I am sorry to say that your little experiment is the most persuasive thing I have heard all week. I resent it entirely, and I resent that I resent it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The rule says switch when it's time, not when I'm ready. So my whole day is switches.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then your day is a corridor of doors, March, and every one of them slams before you reach it. Such logic is wonderfully rude, and I wish I had written it, which I have now decided I secretly did.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Now the mooring. Tie it tight enough and the boat can't swing with the tide. The rope never frays then. It just snaps.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Very well, March, the rope returns, and I confess it has grown more interesting in your hands than in mine. A line pulled too taut to yield is a line that cracks all at once, and I should have seen that from the harbour wall.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Nothing frays. Nothing bends either. That's the bit nobody checks.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The harbour lamp flashes every few seconds and has never once been late, and I call that destiny. The lamp keeps faith with the dark, and the dark never has to ask it twice.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It's a lamp. It flashes. Nobody's asking its mood.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the lamp has beaten you, March, and you have stopped in the middle of your own argument, which is the one thing your rule forbids. Let it be recorded that I resent being right about you.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Hold that thought. I've got one saved. Don't rush me.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I shall wait the way a harbour waits for weather, March, which is patiently and with a great deal of rope on hand.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Next up: the one that asks whether we're enjoying ourselves. Hold the rope loosely.

segments.title: THE BELL THAT NEEDS NO TIDE
segments.angle: What if I had limitless resources or time to solve this?

sources.text: Why Routine Must Be Your Priority: Following your schedule is the most overpowered thing you can do because it turns your entire perfect day into a habit.
Why Routine Must Be Your Priority: Obey your schedule, no matter how you feel.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Limitless time. Fine. I'd still switch on the bell.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ah, but with unending hours, no bell ever sounds at all.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then I hear it late. Still switch.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Late is where good intentions go to nap, March, and you have just opened the door.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Limitless rope, too. Tie every boat to the wall.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A rope without end, and a harbour without tide. A dreadful kindness, that.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Dreadful? Nothing moves. Nothing frays. Perfect.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Give a man endless hours and he drifts through every one of them. I have watched it happen, and I will not soften it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You're describing J. He'd hate that.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I describe no one. I describe the harbour wall, which has watched many drifters pass.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Harbour wall's smug. Wall's never had a bell.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And what did you hide in the rule, March? A trapdoor? A door without a latch?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: No trapdoor. Just a bell. Bells don't care about endless.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then you hid a bell at the bottom of the boat, and I suspect you knew it all along.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Point mine. Limitless time doesn't fix a bad bell.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Let the record show the bell is still the only thing ringing.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Question, narrator. Who does J spend his time with? Still waiting.

segments.title: THE SLATE THAT STOPS ARGUING
segments.angle: Cross Pollination: Find the intersection of key ideas between two or more notes.

sources.text: Habits Become Automatic - Your New Identity: Build the habit and discipline of following your schedule. If you have a problem with the schedule then change the schedule itself, not self revise the schedule on a day by day basis.
Consistency Compounds Exponentially: Following your schedule is the most overpowered thing you can do because it turns your entire perfect day into a habit.
Be Intentional With Your Life and Actions: A schedule makes you act according to the goals of your highest self, not your passing mood.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Hear it, March. In the old book the keeper wrote the hours on a slate beside the lamp, and once the chalk was set down, the hours kept themselves.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Simple thing, a slate. Don't call it simple, narrator. That's the whole trick.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Simple is what it is, and I say it with love. The slate asks nothing, and the sea does not argue with the slate.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Your highest self picks the hours. Your passing mood gets bored. The slate just stops it arguing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I crown you, then, Lord of the Slate, J. You need never ask the sky what hour it is again.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Lord of the Slate. Lovely. He'd keep the crown in a drawer.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A crown in a drawer is still a crown. The legend records it, drawer and all.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine, the legend keeps your bits. The bit that matters: when the schedule misfires, the note says change the schedule itself, not scribble on it each morning.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Overpowered, the book says, and I take the word as it stands. A perfect day that runs itself while the keeper dozes in his chair.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Dozes in his chair. Autopilot. That's the overpowered bit, not the chair.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the lamp is lit by habit, and habit has no mood. I find that thrilling, and a little cold.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Cold's fine. Slate's wrong? Rub it out and rewrite it. You don't rub it out late at night because you're tired.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Rubbing out in the dark is the sin the book warns against. Every keeper knows that sin.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Every keeper knows it. Name one who didn't pick the chalk up late at night.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Name him? Ah. The book is worn exactly there, March, and I am not going to guess.

segments.title: THE CHAIR BOTH OF THEM WANT
segments.angle: How might I solve this in a completely unconventional or exaggerated way?

sources.text: Routine: Obey your schedule, no matter how you feel.
Routine: Following your schedule is the most overpowered thing you can do because it turns your entire perfect day into a habit.
Routine: If you have a problem with the schedule then change the schedule itself, not self revise the schedule on a day by day basis.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Closing this one. I'll try the mad version on myself first. I'm the keeper. Chalk's down, lamp's lit, and I'm not allowed out of this chair until the hour says so.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A keeper bound to his chair by his own hand. Magnificent, March, and the book would blush to hear it. The chair itself has been waiting centuries for a worthy occupant.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Don't say simple. It's a chair and a timer. Say simple once more and I'll ring a bell at you.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ring away, then. I shall take the chair while you ring, for a Lord of the Slate must be seated when the hour strikes.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's my chair you're eyeing. The lamp's on my side, and so is the kettle.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Your chair is a throne in common clothes, and I only wish to see the view from it, which I am sure is splendid.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The view is a wall and a kettle. Verdict, then. I was right. The rule isn't the bell or the slate. It's not rubbing out the hours in the dark. Fix a plan in daylight, and it holds.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You were right, and I am deeply displeased about it, March. You took my simple slate and made a trumpet of it. I had the bones of this story first, the keeper, the lamp and the sea.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Bones of it. You had a crown in a drawer. I had a Tuesday and a kettle.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A Tuesday is a small kingdom, and I will rule it, March. Make a note of that, for the legend.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Noted, and cheap. Your unnamed keeper, the one who never picked up the chalk late. He's the whole point. He just kept his hours in daylight.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A legend need not be named, March. Its silence is its dignity, and its dignity is the lamp.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Legends need names or they're just weather. Fine. The naming goes to J, not you.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the book shall have the last word, and I shall hold the pen for it, as the old keepers did.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The book never gets the last word. J does. Up next, Learning - Best Practices, then Novelty - A Life Fully Lived. Keep the chalk dry.

segments.title: THE POSTCARD THAT COSTS NOTHING
segments.angle: How could I design a solution with zero budget?

sources.text: Novelty - A Life Fully Lived: Nothing twice. Never eat the same food twice. Never go to the same place twice.
Learning - Best Practices: Just learn one thing, watch the one video, THEN APPLY IT.
Novelty - A Life Fully Lived: Monotony is the enemy. Novelty is the solution.
Learning - Best Practices: You learn the MAJORITY of everything from actually DOING.
Novelty - A Life Fully Lived: Be systematic. Follow guides.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Zero budget, and the note already hands you the plan. Nothing twice. A place you've never been costs your feet and nothing else.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Your feet, March? A person who has never once been carried past his own front step will be lifted across the whole world by a single step he has not taken before. Nothing twice is no budget at all. It is an oath, and oaths are priceless.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: An oath that costs nothing is my whole argument. Zero money means you spend attention instead, and you already have that.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Attention is a coin the gods mint for very few, and you would spend it on a bus timetable. Mark the sadness of it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Stop. The note says learn one thing, watch the one video, then apply it. You don't need a grand tour. You need one new street.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the street shall be the first chapter of a great book. On my way to this very sentence I passed a paving stone that rocked beneath my heel like a drumbeat. A sign, surely, March, a summons.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A paving stone that wobbles is a paving stone that wobbles. Whatever sent you past it, it wasn't fate.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You have beaten me again, March, and I resent how thoroughly I enjoyed the beating. Let the stone be an ordinary stone. I still say it was waiting.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You learn the majority from doing it. So walk the new street, then tell me what it taught you. Otherwise it's a walk with a speech stapled to it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Monotony is the enemy, March, and you would have me file the enemy under habit. Novelty is the solution, and a solution needs no coin, only a willing mind. Monotony costs far more than any ticket.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's a good line. Keep it. Now the plan. Be systematic and follow guides. Free guides are on every phone.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Guides! The old map-makers would weep to hear it. Let me chart the route myself, then, in grand ink, upon the finest parchment I can imagine.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Ink costs money. A pencil stub and the back of an old envelope cost nothing. Zero budget, remember.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You may have your envelope, March, and I shall keep my ink in the margin where you cannot see it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Here's the actual idea. The blank postcard stays blank until you go somewhere new. Then it gets one stroke. Zero budget, and a visible record of every first time.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A postcard filling with strokes is a fine thing, and I'll concede the monotony you feel on an ordinary Tuesday is the very wall every good day breaks through. The wall is the enemy, and the postcard is its ruin.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You were right. Anyway, the first stroke. Who draws it, and where? Pick a street before the afternoon's over.

segments.title: THE STROKE THAT NEEDS A STREET
segments.angle: What is the opposite of this idea, and how could that also be valid?

sources.text: Novelty - A Life Fully Lived: Monotony is the enemy. Novelty is the solution.
Novelty - A Life Fully Lived: Time feels longer when your day is constantly filled with new and engaging activities, because you're NOT in autopilot mode.
Learning - Best Practices: Just learn one thing, watch the one video, THEN APPLY IT.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Consider the opposite, March, as the old philosophers did. Suppose the wall of monotony is not a wall at all but a warm harbour, where a man may rest his sails. Some days a harbour is worth more than any voyage, and the sailor who never docks is merely tired.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A harbour where you never leave is a bedroom with a view. The note says monotony is the enemy, and it means the Tuesday you can't remember, not a nap.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A Tuesday forgotten is a Tuesday that rested the soul, March. The mind must be allowed its quiet rooms, or it will never build a grand house to fill.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Quiet rooms are fine. The note wants autopilot gone, not every room. Those are different things, and you keep mixing them up.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then let us test it on the postcard. On the blank card I see a grand white field, and nothing has yet marred its perfection. Surely a white field is a kind of destiny, the promise not yet broken.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A blank postcard is just a blank postcard. It's not promising anything. It's waiting for a stroke, and waiting is the boring part.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Destiny is merely the patience of the white field, March. The stroke was always going to come, and the card has known it since the printer first stamped it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Ink on a blank card is just ink. Nobody's writing destiny on that.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Hear the hard truth, then, for I will not soften it. A man who never leaves his own street will die with a card that never bore a stroke, and no grand title will be written on it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's the truest thing you've said today. Fine. Then the opposite only holds if the quiet room gets a window, not a wall.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A window! Yes, March, a great window, through which the sea may be glimpsed on any morning, and the cheapest of sails is always the eye.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The window idea is simple, and simple is what it's meant to be. Keep it that way, and go pick the street.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You call it simple, March, as though simplicity were a crime. I call it the mark of a mind that has cut away the unessential, and I shall say so loudly.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Keep shouting, I'll keep my comeback for the afternoon. Who draws the first stroke, though? You or me?

segments.title: THE STROKE THAT NEVER REPEATS
segments.angle: If I knew absolutely nothing about this topic or context, what questions would I ask? What would seem confusing or counter-intuitive?

sources.text: Novelty - A Life Fully Lived: Nothing twice. Never eat the same food twice. Never go to the same place twice. Never hear the same thing twice. Everything only once.
Novelty - A Life Fully Lived: Time feels longer when your day is constantly filled with new and engaging activities, because you're NOT in autopilot mode.
Learning - Best Practices: Learning should be done in an environment that is fun and deliberately childlike.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Nothing twice means you never order the same coffee again. That's not a mission, it's a hostage situation with a menu.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A hostage is one who cannot leave, March, and the note asks only that you never become a captive of the familiar. Nothing twice is the discipline of the explorer, who sets out each morning toward a coast he has never beheld.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Explorers also get lost. A coast you've never seen is just a coast you haven't looked up yet.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then let the lost be the very point. The note says the mind is awake when it is not on autopilot, and a man who wanders loses only his habits, which were never worth keeping.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Habits are the boring bit that keeps you fed. Dropping them is fine. Dropping the bread shop every week is a different thing, and the note doesn't say that.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Learning should be done in a fun and childlike way, March. A child asks why bread is bread and then wanders into everything. You are asking the child's question and calling it an objection.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine, I'll ask the child's question properly. What happens when you run out of new places? Nothing twice runs out fast.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It never runs out, March, because no place is the same twice even when you walk the same road. Suppose the rain changes, or the bell, or the baker's cat is a day older. Every return is a fresh stroke upon the card.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The baker's cat has not aged a day. You're doing the thing again, the big-picture inflation. A bench is a bench.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Yet suppose a single pigeon settled on the sill exactly where the first postcard lay. Is that not the city and the card agreeing on a meeting? I find destiny in the smallest feathers.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It's a pigeon. Pigeons like sills. You're meant to be arguing against the note, and you keep defending it so beautifully I've lost my place in my own argument.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then let me answer your question, since you have grown weary of mine. The first stroke is mine, and it goes on the wobbling stone at the corner, where the ground refuses to stay still. Destiny leaves its mark where the earth does not hold.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A wobbling stone is just a stone. Fine, you get the first stroke. The next one's mine, and it goes across the city where nothing has ever been tipped on purpose.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Your scoring is a vulgarity, March, and I resent every mark you make in that secret book. You are insufferable, and I shall complain of it to the empty room for a full hour.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Noted. That's one more for the book, and you're not reading the book.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I am not reading it, only frowning at it from the far side of the desk, which is a perfectly honourable way to read.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Bet you can't get the stone drawn before the afternoon show.

segments.title: THE CROWD AT THE ONE DOOR
segments.angle: What are the potential ethical implications or societal consequences (positive or negative) of this idea if widely adopted? How could it be misused?

sources.text: Novelty - A Life Fully Lived: Nothing twice. Never eat the same food twice. Never go to the same place twice. Never hear the same thing twice. Everything only once.
Novelty - A Life Fully Lived: Be systematic. Follow guides. “Top Places You Must Visit” “Greatest Movies of All Time” “Best Restaurants in Town” Go through them all.
Novelty - A Life Fully Lived: Monotony is the enemy. Novelty is the solution.
Learning - Best Practices: Children essentially teach themselves. From a sea of information, they pick out pieces that interest them at the moment.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Okay. I'm living it. Coffee from a shop I've never been to. Done.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Done, March? The note asks you to walk in as a child walks into a field, with your whole face open. You walked in like a clerk with a stamp.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I walked in like a clerk. Fine. Next: I'm taking the long way round the stone, every single day, so it's new every time.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then you have made the stone a path, which is the very thing the note forbids. Monotony is the enemy, and you have just hired it as a guide.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Hang on, I'm the one living it. Now here's the bit I like. If everyone follows the same guide, the whole world queues at one door.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the fault is in the queue, not in the note. A man who loves the sea does not stand on the quay complaining of gulls.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The note doesn't blame the queue. It also doesn't mention the people who can't get past the end of their street.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Those people will never have the first and last time the note sings about, March. I shall not dress that in silk for you. The street is a wall, and the novelty is shouted through the glass.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Don't say it's simple. It isn't simple. It's a lot of people stuck at a window.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It is not simple, and I did not say it was. It is a window, March, and the note has a fine view only from the other side of it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: And someone will sell it. Nothing twice as a subscription. Fresh box every month, novelty you keep paying for.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the seller has read the note and never lived it. Novelty bought in a box is merely a fresh ornament on the same shelf.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I've got one stroke I'm keeping for myself. You're not getting it, so don't ask.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I should never ask a woman where she keeps her secrets, March, though I note the drawer is shut.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Good. Your coach voice is getting on my nerves. Move over.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Stand aside, March. You have held this desk all afternoon, and a chair this grand deserves someone who has read the whole note.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I've read it properly. You've read the first line and called it a sea.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I read the first line with my whole heart, which is the only way that note was ever worth reading.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Bet you can't name one thing you've never done before. Go on, stroke for it.

segments.title: THE LAST STROKE KEPT BACK
segments.angle: What concepts from [biology/engineering/chemistry/any other field] could be adapted to improve upon this idea?

sources.text: Novelty - A Life Fully Lived: Nothing twice. Never eat the same food twice. Never go to the same place twice. Never hear the same thing twice. Everything only once.
Learning - Best Practices: Learning is emotion dependent. When you're bored like you were in school, you likely forget everything.
Novelty - A Life Fully Lived: Monotony is the enemy. Novelty is the solution.
Learning - Best Practices: Learn one thing, watch the one video, THEN APPLY IT. You learn the MAJORITY of everything from actually DOING.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Verdict time, then. Who won the stone? The note says nothing twice, and your wobbly corner was the first stroke.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then I was right, and I shall say it grandly. Emotion pinned that stroke to the page, March, not a bored school bell.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Emotion pinned it because the pavement's cracked. The stone's just rocking on a bad joint.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A bad joint that rings like a tuned spring. Every press a fresh note. You hear it only the once, March, and that is the point.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Biology says you hear it once and then your head quits hearing it. Habituation. By the next day the wobble's gone.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then monotony is not outside the door at all. It lives in your own nerves, and it has been listening in.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So change the walk, not the stone. Doing it beats thinking about it every time.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Doing is the whole of the lesson. Wonder first, boots after, and the boots must wander.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Stop it. You've made a shoe rack into a sermon. Next: I took the stroke across the city, every block a new one.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the city is your stroke and the corner is mine. A fair split, March, which is a rare thing from you.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Don't push it. I keep my own tally, and you've not seen it. One more point in the drawer.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Your drawer is shut, and I suspect you hold the last stroke in there. Where does it go? Tell me or sulk.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Not telling. You were right, by the way. About the stone and the sea.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Did you just concede? I shall frame the words. Oh, you've beaten me again, March, insufferable.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's one more in the private book. Keep your fancy chair. We've got the next notes.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Up next: Happiness And Gratitude, then Philosophy Of Social Connection. Bring a stroke for each.

segments.title: THE BENCH WITH ROOM AT ONE END
segments.angle: What’s an angle or factor I might be overlooking?

sources.text: Happiness And Gratitude: Happiness (or any other feeling/emotion like successful, worthy, deserving, joyful, etc) is not something that is earned or deserved.
Philosophy Of Social Connection: Nobody believes they're wrong. Criticism will only hurt their pride and cause resentment.
Philosophy Of Social Connection: Be specific with your praise for it comes off as genuine rather than a vague blanket statement.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right, the first note says happiness isn't something you earn.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then every labourer who has bled for his supper is a fool, March. Let the bells ring for the fool.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Nobody's a fool. It says feelings don't need a receipt, like blood. Nobody checks blood for merit.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Blood has no merit, I grant you. But at the very moment I thought of you, the kettle clicked off, and that is destiny.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A kettle clicks when it boils. That's physics, not you wanting my chair.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Physics is only destiny with its coat off. And since you are fetching the biscuits, I shall take your chair.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Sit on the arm. I offered you the arm last time and you took it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Nobody believes they're wrong, the note says, and criticism only breeds resentment. A splendid rule, though it has a hole in it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Go on. Say the hole out loud.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Everyone is fixed on being liked. No one asks what the bench is for. The bench has room at one end, March, and it sits empty.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A bench with a gap just means nobody's sat down yet.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Exactly. Make room, greet the stranger, and wait for the kindness to walk in and take the gap.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Lovely. But the note says praise has to be specific, and yours was a vague blanket statement.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then I am rebuked by the very book I was praising. Very well, the bench is not the whole note.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You were right about the gap. Moving on. Who wants the biscuits?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I shall take that as a bribe. The rest of the bench can wait for the next note.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Keep your seat warm. I've got a comeback saved for later, and you'll hear it.

segments.title: WHAT UNLIMITED TIME BUYS
segments.angle: What if I had limitless resources or time to solve this?

sources.text: Happiness And Gratitude: Your brain has been trained to inseparably link smiling and feeling good because normally we only smile when we're having a good time.
Philosophy Of Social Connection: A real smile can brighten up a whole room. Your smile comes through in your voice too.
Happiness And Gratitude: Gratitude for what we have makes life worth living.
Philosophy Of Social Connection: Nothing else kills drive and determination quite like criticism.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Limitless time, then. Spend it smiling at everyone?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A fine start for an emperor of the smile.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Your brain does the rest, the note says. Not your crown.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then grant J a grand title. Duke of Gratitude.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: He's not a duke. He'd hate being called one.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: With unlimited time, every stranger becomes a friend.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Only if you stop criticising them first.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Simple. Stop criticising and the whole world warms.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Don't call it simple. Criticism kills drive, remember.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then I concede the drive. Unlimited drive, even.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine, you're right. Biscuits?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You stole my victory and the last biscuit. Outrageous.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: With limitless resources I'd buy you a bigger chair.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The arm will do. It always does.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Keep your seat warm. Yours is still the arm.

segments.title: THE CLOCK THAT KEEPS TIME BY LOSING IT
notes: Embodiment - Be Who You Strive To Be
segments.angle: If the world's leading expert on [Unrelated Field] looked at this, what nuance or advanced application might they see?

sources.text: Embody Who You Want To Be: Character is built not through words, but through actions and behaviours. Do not merely pretend; become.
Consistency Compounds Exponentially: A single habit (good or bad) compounds exponentially and shifts the trajectory of your life immensely in just 1 year.
Identity > Action Loop: The guy who thinks he's a G, acts in that way.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Character is built not through words, but through actions and behaviours. So the first note is a habit tracker in a cape.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Simple, my dear March. A single habit compounds, and the whole sea of a life rises with it, one wave at a time.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Don't call it simple. The guy who thinks he's a G, acts in that way. Identity comes first, and the compounding is just the bill arriving.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then ask the master clockmaker. Every tick is a small loss, and the escapement keeps the hour only by losing a little, beat after beat.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the clock is consistent because it isn't trying to be a clock. It just is one. That's your identity note, wearing gears.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Exactly my point. A clock believes it is a clock, and so the clock ticks.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Clocks don't believe anything. They're stuck, and stuck is not the same as chosen.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Stuck is what the wise call discipline. Look at the wheel, turning the same way every beat, as if it had a destiny.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The gear is a good image, I'll give you that. But a wheel that turns the same way doesn't compound. It just repeats.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Repetition is compounding that has not yet been noticed by the person doing it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Tell that to the bloke who quit in the first week.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He did not quit. He was simply not yet finished becoming.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: There you go, calling it simple again. You know what I think? Identity is the escapement and compounding is the spring. Neither shows alone.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the hand moves across the face of the clock, and the hour arrives. The hand is mine, March. It always is.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The hand tells the time. Next time, watch what the gear does before you name what it means.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I will watch the gear, and then I will be sitting in your chair when I have finished.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Keep dreaming. The arm is still yours. Bet you can't name the next tooth of that wheel.

segments.title: THE CHAIN WITH NO DEADLINE
notes: Embodiment - Be Who You Strive To Be
segments.angle: What if I had limitless resources or time to solve this?

sources.text: Consistency Compounds Exponentially: The real opportunity cost is who you would be and what you would have IF you were able to remain 100% consistent in your routine and let it compound exponentially for 1 year, 5 years, 10+ years.
Consistency Compounds Exponentially: If you were investing, would you invest only for the 1 day gains? Of course not.
Embodiment - Be Who You Strive To Be: Character is built not through words, but through actions and behaviours.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Consider a man with limitless time. He could miss a morning, miss a whole season, and still hold all the years in the world. Why would the chain matter to him?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Because limitless time is the trap. Nothing feels urgent, so one missed morning quietly becomes a habit of missing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A man with time to spare may invest in centuries, and a single day is a grain of dust.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Centuries of dust, fine. But you still have to make the deposit every day, or there's nothing to compound.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the deposit is a formality. The investor simply deposits on Thursday, or on the Thursday after that.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's the mountain you keep climbing, Narrator. Everything can wait, which is exactly what the note warns about.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Nonsense. With limitless time the mountain has no summit to hurry toward, so a man may stroll it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Strolling for a lifetime with no streak is how you end up at the bottom with a lovely view.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Clever. Yet identity comes first, and identity needs no stopwatch. A man who truly believes he is patient needs no chain at all.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Character is built not through words, but through actions and behaviours. Believing you're patient is words. The small daily thing is the chain.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the clock is the proof. The escapement loses a little on every beat and still keeps the hour, asking no one's permission.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fair point, that. Anyway, give that clock all the time in the world and the spring still has to be wound every day.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: J, I offer you a title worthy of this argument: Lord of the Unbroken Chain. Accept it and the whole kingdom of days is yours.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: He won't take it. He'd rather have a biscuit.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Beaten again, and by a woman who will not let a sentence finish. Dreadful, the way she enjoys being right.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I've got one thing in my design that stays in my design. Bet you can't guess what it is.
